episodes.215142: On the 11-15th, several rounds of heavy to extreme rainfall within the upper White River watershed led to major flooding from Muncie to Indianapolis on both the White River and several tributaries.  One-day rainfall amounts:  through the early morning of the 12th were as great as 4-8 inches across all watershed areas east of Anderson; through the early morning of the 13th were up to 2-5 inches for most areas near and east of Anderson; with subsequent, less intense rains focused from the Tipton to Anderson areas;  leading to widespread 5-day totals through the 15th evening of 5-10 inches from northern Marion County to all watershed points north and east, including a large area of 9-13 inches from Anderson to the White River's easternmost headwaters in Randolph County.||Resultant major flooding impacted all points on the upper White River from Muncie down to Ravenswood, with the crest advancing from Muncie on the 13th midday to Ravenswood by the 15th late day;  including record crests at both Anderson (24.93 feet, surpassing 23.60 from 3/23/1904) and Noblesville (24.60 feet, surpassing 23.80 from 3/25/1913).  Significant flooding was ubiquitous over several White River tributaries, including crests in major flood on Fall Creek at Fortville (13th evening) and Cicero Creek at Arcadia (15th late day).||Flooding impacts ranged from evacuations in the Muncie and Indianapolis areas, to submerged roadways and highways in Delaware County and the Anderson and Edgewood parts of Madison County;  and inundated residential neighborhoods in Muncie, Yorktown, Riverwood, Noblesville, Federal Hill, low-lying portions of Fishers and Carmel, Ravenswood, Rocky Ripple and near Broad Ripple.  Ninety swift water rescues were needed in Hamilton County, and emergency floodgate operations were needed in northern Marion County. Approximately 2,500 structures were impacted across Delaware, Hamilton, Madison and Marion Counties.  Most notably the White River in Carmel flooded back up Blue Woods Creek, washing out the Hazel Dell Parkway bridge and overflowing as a waterfall into the Martin Marietta - North Indianapolis Mine.  Two fatalities occurred in Delaware County.||Outside of the broader river flooding, a culvert washout caused a fatality in Henry County after the flash flooding ended when a bicycler rode into the collapsed road and perished.
episodes.215448: Hurricane Lala formed in the central Pacific and approached the islands from southeast. The hurricane passed just south of the Big Island, then moved northwest and passed south of the rest of the Hawaiian islands. Lala brought catastrophic damage to the Big Island of Hawaii in the form of massive flooding and wind damage. Considerable widespread damage due to the winds and flooding was also felt over the rest of the islands.
episodes.215499: During the 15th morning and early afternoon, a humid, unstable airmass and a slow-moving surface boundary fueled multiple rounds of heavy rainfall across central Indiana. High atmospheric moisture content combined with training thunderstorm activity led to intense rainfall rates over soils already saturated from previous precipitation events over the previous days.||Flooding commenced around 06:45 EST in western portions of the region before expanding eastward through Marion, Hamilton, Tipton, and Delaware counties into the mid-afternoon. Overall rainfall totals averaged between 1 and 2.5 inches across much of the central corridor, while localized totals reached up to 4.5 inches in Fountain County from late August 14 through August 15.||Rapid runoff generated widespread flash flooding and nuisance areal flooding across impacted counties. Deep standing water submerged multiple state routes and local roadways, causing vehicle submersions, road washouts, and mandatory closures. Active water rescues were conducted near inundated commercial areas, while overflowing waterways, including the White River, flooded adjacent grounds, residential yards, and riverfront facilities before high water receded late in the day.

episodes.216135: Convergence on a surface trough and upslope flow yielded thunderstorm development in southeast New Mexico and in the higher terrain of west Texas. A couple of storms produced severe winds, and flash flooding was reported near Terlingua Ranch.
episodes.216167: A stalled frontal boundary and a very moist airmass combined to produce training thunderstorms and torrential rainfall near the I-74 corridor during the morning of August 15th.  Rainfall amounts of 4-7 inches were common, which caused flash flooding from Fulton County eastward through Vermilion County.  Two flood deaths occurred when vehicles were swept into flooded field ditches in Champaign and Vermilion counties.
episodes.216244: Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued into the middle of August as a front remained in the vicinity on the 15th, lifted north as a warm front on the 16th, and then a cold front passed through on the 17th. ||Some strong to severe thunderstorms were noted during this timeframe, with daily observations of downed trees and power lines in northeast Kentucky from the 15th to the 17th. 72-hour rainfall amounts generally ranged from one to three inches, although some pockets of three to five inches were observed. Seemingly endless rounds of precipitation during the first half of the month had already saturated soils across much of the area. Thus, even lesser rainfall amounts were needed to cause some roadway flooding in northeast Kentucky.
episodes.216246: Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued in West Virginia as a front remained in the vicinity on August 15th, lifted north as a warm front on the 16th, and then a cold front passed through on the 17th. 72-hour rainfall amounts generally ranged from one to three inches, though some pockets of three to five inches were observed. Seemingly endless rounds of precipitation during the first half of the month had already saturated soils across much of the area. Thus, even lesser rainfall amounts resulted in flooded roads across portions of West Virginia. Impacts from heavier rain also included water rescues, flooded structures, and river flooding on Clear Fork, Sand Run, Elk Twomile Creek, Tygart Valley River, West Fork River, and Middle Island Creek. Additionally, episodic rounds of strong thunderstorms produced during this timeframe resulted in more downed trees and power lines across the state. This occurred in locations that had already faced powerful storms earlier in the month, adding to the total of storm damage costs.

episodes.218239: During the late afternoon and evening hours of August 15th, isolated showers and thunderstorms developed and progressed over north central Kentucky near the Bluegrass region. With afternoon high temperatures in the 90s and dew points in the low-to-mid 70s, this helped produce MLCAPE values up to around 2500-3000 J/kg. While weaker wind shear did limit the extent of convective development, the higher instability and ample moisture in the form of PW greater than 2 did result in isolated thunderstorm wind damage and flash flooding. During the late afternoon through the late evening hours of the 16th, scattered thunderstorms moved over southern Indiana and north central Kentucky ahead of a cold front passing through the Ohio Valley. While there was meager deep-layer shear in place, a 30-40 kt LLJ, ample instability of MLCAPE around 2500-3000 J/kg, and decent moisture with PW over 1.8 helped result in some thunderstorms producing severe wind gusts and damage.

Intense rainbands associated with the eyewall of Lala produced extreme rainfall rates during the evening of Saturday, August 15th through most of Sunday, August 16th. The highest rainfall totals were observed over the southeast slopes of the Big Island in the Kau District. Massive flood waves surged through Naalehu and Pahala, effectively cutting off the towns, sweeping homes off of their foundations, and destroying bridges, roads, and other vital infrastructure. Two direct fatalities were reported in Naalehu as a result of the flooding. Many other valuable community assets, such as schools and the Naalehu cemetery, were damaged. Grave sites and human remains were washed away in swift moving flood waters. Roads were washed out, exposing underground power lines and leaving massive trenches. In total, six bridges were either destroyed or severely damaged, and around thirty roads were closed. Search and rescue teams saved an elderly woman and a paramedic team from the flood waters.
